# Open Problems Worth a Frontier-Model Run — Final Ranked Report

**Prospecting target:** genuine open questions with mechanically checkable outcomes.
**Scoring:** 35 points across verifiability (V), certificate size (C), untried angle (U), barrier clarity (B), reformulation surface (R), partial credit (P), decomposability (D). Adjusted total applies the skeptic's penalty.

**How to read this.** Every entry below survived a refutation pass, and most survived with damage. Where a skeptic offered a salvage, **the salvaged framing is the one written into the theory of attack** — the original pitch is preserved only where it explains what not to do. Read the objections before the first move, not after. The single most common failure mode in this batch was a pitch whose positive branch ("find a new object") turned out to be the output of a published algorithm; the surviving value is almost always in the negative branch ("certify no such object exists in this class").

**Two kinds of pick.** Some of these are near-certain to produce a publishable object even if the headline result never lands (#4, #6, #9, #10). Others survived on the strength of exactly one idea and will produce nothing if that idea fails (#3, #5, #8, #11). This is flagged per entry as **Yield**. Do not pick a long shot expecting partial credit.

## Tier 1 — Best structural fit

### 1. Non-solvability certificates for free-fermion-in-disguise Hamiltonians
**Adjusted 24** (raw 32) · V5 C4 U4 B5 R4 P5 D5

**Problem.** The "free fermions in disguise" (FFD) program has a growing body of *sufficient* graph-theoretic conditions for when a spin Hamiltonian's frustration graph admits a free-fermion solution — Elman–Chapman–Flammia's even-hole-and-claw-free (ECF) class, then Chapman–Elman–Mann's strictly larger simplicial-claw-free (SCF) class (arXiv:2305.15625), then twin-collapse extensions (arXiv:2509.09092), and the 2026 graph-Clifford "generalized free fermions" line (arXiv:2602.03431, 2605.31453). There is **zero necessity machinery**. Nobody can point at a concrete frustration graph and prove no coupling vector makes it solvable.

**Theory of attack (salvaged — moments, not spectra).** Do not enumerate spectra and do not chase new solvable models; both branches are already automated (see objections). Commit entirely to the obstruction direction, for a *fixed* small graph outside SCF. The workable formulation is via **traces, not eigenvalues**: `tr(H^{2k})` is a signed closed-walk count on the frustration graph, computable combinatorially in the couplings with no diagonalization, no Hilbert space, and no representation-multiplicity ambiguity. A free-fermion spectrum forces `tr(exp(-βH)) = Π 2cosh(β ε_i)`, which after eliminating the `ε_i` by Newton's identities becomes an explicit finite set of polynomial relations among the low moments in the coupling ring. That converts an existential real-quantifier-elimination problem (which is doubly exponential and will not terminate) into **ideal membership at fixed low degree** — well-conditioned, terminating, and producing exactly the page-scale printable certificate the field lacks.

**First move.** Build the moment machinery and validate before trusting anything: reproduce the claw-and-even-hole-containing solvable model of arXiv:2508.05789 as satisfying the moment relations, and reproduce SCF-sufficient graphs as satisfying them. Only then run the ideal-membership test on graphs outside SCF, smallest first.

**Kill condition.** If the pipeline cannot reproduce arXiv:2508.05789 as solvable, the graph-to-moment realization is wrong and nothing downstream means anything — stop. If ideal membership at low degree is inconclusive on every small non-SCF graph (relations always satisfiable, no obstruction surfaces at any reachable degree), the moment route has no teeth and the problem reverts to real QE, which is out of reach.

**Surviving objections you are walking into.**
- The positive half of the original pitch is dead three times over. arXiv:2509.09092 is literally a recursive graph-search algorithm that finds solvable models outside the known classes. A "new FFD model" is not a result; it is an instance of a published algorithm's output. Do not spend a minute there.
- The naive spectral test (`±`-sum of n/2 numbers) attacks the wrong property. Free-fermion solvability is a statement about the operator algebra — existence of a Majorana-bilinear image — not about the spectrum. At small n the spectral condition is satisfiable by accident, and the number of modes and their multiplicities are not determined by the frustration graph, so the test has undetermined arity: false positives at small n, false negatives under multiplicity. This is why the run must go through moments.
- Random couplings only detect *generic* solvability, which is the already-classified case. The interesting fine-tuned cases are measure-zero. Any numeric pass is decoration.
- Definitional drift is a live risk: the 2026 generalized-free-fermion papers keep widening what counts as solvable. Frame the deliverable narrowly — "no Majorana-bilinear solution in the standard sense for graph G" — and state the definition in the certificate.

**Yield: high.** Even one concrete graph with a machine-checkable non-solvability certificate is the first such object in the field. The pipeline itself (combinatorial moments from frustration graphs) is reusable and publishable as tooling. This is the only entry where the salvaged plan is both novel and computationally sane.

### 2. Order of finite weak central groupoids (ETP law E1485) is n² or 2n²
**Adjusted 19** (raw 27) · V5 C5 U3 B4 R4 P3 D3

**Problem.** The Equational Theories Project observed empirically that every finite model of law E1485 (weak central groupoids) has order n² or 2n². The final ETP paper (arXiv:2512.07087) states plainly: "we have no rigorous proof of this claim." Knuth proved the analogous theorem for genuine central groupoids (A² = J forces order n²); the weak law relaxes the equality to a path-existence condition.

**Theory of attack (salvaged — structure theorem, not trace identity).** The disjunction is the tell. A single polynomial identity in the adjacency matrix A and the all-ones matrix J cannot produce a disjunctive conclusion; a disjunction has to come from a case split — a Z/2 grading, a fixed-point-free involution, a double cover. So the right conjecture is the structure theorem the empirical pattern is *reporting*: **every finite weak central groupoid is either a central groupoid (order n²) or a Z/2-cover of one (order 2n²)**. That single mechanism explains both branches and is immediately testable against the two known models.

**First move.** Take the ETP blueprint's order-2 NAND magma on F₂ and the order-32 model (M₂^⊗5 twisted by an order-5 automorphism) and try to exhibit an explicit 2-to-1 morphism onto a central groupoid of order 1 and 16 respectively. That is a same-day check with a decisive outcome. **Skip the small-order SAT enumeration** — the ETP has a dedicated "Enumerating Small Finite Magmas" chapter and ran finite model finders across the corpus; orders 3, 5, 6, 7 are already settled and are the source of the empirical claim itself. Check the repo's enumeration output before writing any encoder.

**Kill condition.** If neither known model admits a 2-to-1 morphism onto a central groupoid, the covering mechanism is wrong and the disjunction has no visible source — and the fallback (find a polynomial identity in A and J common to all known models) is the route the skeptic argues cannot produce a disjunction anyway. Both dead inside a day.

**Surviving objections.**
- "Nobody with an algebraic toolkit has looked at this" is false as of 2026. E1485 is the project's self-described "final boss," with an active named group including ring theorists (Jose Brox, Pace Nielsen) reporting "significant progress" on structure theory. Read the 2026 Zulip thread output before starting; that is where any structure theory already lives.
- The refutation arm is mispriced. Orders 10–15 are where non-existence becomes genuinely hard: full lex-leader symmetry breaking needs the S_n conjugation action (12! ≈ 5×10⁸), so only partial symmetry breaking is encodable, and the residual search over 12^144 to 15^225 cells is not an afternoon. If you do search, search over the **digraph formulation with the good-path structure imposed**, not raw multiplication tables — that is the only reduction that plausibly reaches order 12–15.
- Entrywise positivity of A² constrains rank not at all, which is precisely why Knuth's argument does not transfer.

**Yield: medium.** The covering-theorem check is cheap and decisive. If it lands, the proof is a real theorem with an existing Lean statement to check against. If it does not, there is no consolation prize here.

## Tier 2 — Real cracks, narrow margins

### 3. Completing the Shiraishi–Yamaguchi integrability classification beyond spin S = 13.5
**Adjusted 18** (raw 26) · V4 C4 U3 B4 R4 P3 D4

**Problem.** Shiraishi–Yamaguchi's dichotomy theorem (arXiv:2504.14315, Phys. Rev. B 2026) holds for general spin S, but the *complete classification* of isotropic integrable spin-S chains is validated only to S ≤ 13.5. The paper explicitly leaves open whether all integrable models above that are within the scope of the Yang–Baxter equation. The classification's shape below 13.5 is four infinite sequences (corresponding to four series of compact Lie groups) **plus one exceptional solution at S = 3**.

**Theory of attack (salvaged — follow the exceptional case).** Do not chase a recursion in S. The infinite families are already explained representation-theoretically, which is a stronger structure than a recursion; the residual open content is entirely about **sporadic** solutions, and sporadic solutions by construction do not satisfy recursions — S = 3 is the proof of that. Instead: the S = 3 exceptional case says sporadic Reshetikhin solutions come from exceptional structure. The exceptional compact Lie algebras are a finite list (G₂, F₄, E₆, E₇, E₈) with a finite list of representations embeddable in an isotropic spin-S chain. **Enumerate those embeddings and check each against the Reshetikhin condition directly.** That is finite, complete, self-certifying, and would close the sporadic question for *all* S rather than advancing the frontier by one spin. Complementary second shot: use Ponzano–Regge semiclassical asymptotics of the 6j symbols to prove non-existence of new solutions for all S above some S₀, which combined with the computed range S ≤ 13.5 finishes the classification outright.

**First move.** Enumerate the exceptional-algebra representations of dimension 2S+1 for S in the accessible range and above, write the Reshetikhin condition for each embedding, and verify the machinery reproduces the known S = 3 exceptional solution before trusting any new case.

**Kill condition.** If the exceptional-embedding enumeration reproduces only the known S = 3 case and yields no other candidate embeddings at any S, the sporadic route yields a (small, honest) completeness statement and nothing more — bank it and stop. If the machinery cannot reproduce S = 3, it is wrong.

**Surviving objections.**
- The original "untried angle" was not untried and its premise was false. The projector basis with 6j/Racah recoupling is how Kennedy and Batchelor–Yung already write these searches — textbook Kulish–Reshetikhin–Sklyanin material. And 6j symbols are **not rational functions of S**: Racah's sum formula gives alternating sums of factorial ratios times a square-root normalization, a hypergeometric term. The square roots alone break the polynomial-recursion picture. The original pitch's own kill condition fires on the first derivation.
- The fallback (brute-force Gröbner elimination at S = 14, 15) buys one or two spins of a computation a well-resourced group already pushed to its economic limit, and is at risk of commoditisation by the single-conservation-law reduction line (arXiv:2508.20713).
- Fast-moving competitors: Shiraishi–Yamaguchi shipped three papers in under a year.

**Yield: low-medium, long shot.** This entry survives on one idea (exceptional algebras generate the sporadic solutions). If that idea is right the payoff is large and clean; if wrong, there is no fallback that is not already commoditised.

### 4. Certified optimality of the Chen–Engel–Glotzer tetrahedron packing
**Adjusted 17** (raw 29) · V5 C5 U4 B4 R4 P3 D4

**Problem.** The densest known packing of regular tetrahedra is 4000/4671 ≈ 0.856347 (Chen–Engel–Glotzer 2010), and nothing has beaten it in sixteen years. Its optimality is **not proved** — CEG's own claim is explicitly numerical: the packing "has maximal density within a three-parameter family of dimer packings, and numerical compressions starting from random configurations *suggest* that the packing may be optimal at least for small cells with up to 16 tetrahedra."

**Theory of attack (salvaged — prove a theorem, do not hunt a record).** The record hunt is dead as pitched (see objections). Point the same exact machinery at a theorem instead: **a computer-assisted proof that 4000/4671 is optimal among all periodic packings with at most k tetrahedra per fundamental cell**, for the largest k reachable. Exact algebraic lattice vectors, separating-plane certificates over a finite neighbour shell, interval arithmetic on the parameter sweep. This converts CEG's heuristic "suggests optimal for small cells" into something proved, and it is exactly the finite rigorous case analysis the certificate story is built for. Secondary target, also real: the exact local-optimality certificate for the CEG dimer packing over its three-parameter family plus a certified neighbour shell.

**First move.** Implement or port Betke–Henk for 3-polytopes and validate by reproducing the known optimal lattice packing density of the triangular dipyramid — it must return exactly 4000/4671. Then set up the interval-arithmetic parameter sweep for k = 2 (dimer) and establish the certified local-optimality statement before attempting any larger k.

**Kill condition.** If Betke–Henk cannot reproduce 4000/4671 on the dipyramid, the tool is untrustworthy and everything downstream is noise. If the certified sweep cannot close even the k = 2 three-parameter family within interval arithmetic, larger k is hopeless and the theorem framing dies too.

**Surviving objections.**
- The original record-hunting plan (lattice-pack the convex hulls of k = 3..6 clusters) is strictly *inside* a region CEG already swept, since a cluster-lattice packing of k tetrahedra is a periodic packing with k tetrahedra per cell, and 3–6 ≪ 16. Kallus–Elser–Gravel and Torquato–Jiao ran comparable searches over the same regime.
- Packing convex hulls instead of tetrahedra can only *lose* density: it forbids the interpenetration of concave complements that is exactly where dense tetrahedron packings get their density.
- The original one-hour kill condition (fill fraction below 0.90) **will not fire**, which is bad news: the five-tetrahedron ring about a common edge has hull fill fraction ≈ 0.97–0.98 (the angular deficit is only 7.36°). A run using that kill condition passes its own check and then burns its budget re-deriving a 2010 negative. These same wagon-wheel motifs are what Chen's 0.7786 and Torquato–Jiao's packings were built from, and they underperformed the dimer.
- Betke–Henk is not free: it enumerates over facet/difference-body combinations and its cost explodes for hulls with many vertices — exactly what larger clusters produce. Expect k to stay small.

**Yield: high for the theorem, ~zero for the record.** If you pick this up, pick it up as a certification project. Optimality-in-a-class is all partial credit; the record framing has none.

### 5. Spectral gap of the spin-2 AKLT model on the square lattice
**Adjusted 17** (raw 25) · V4 C4 U2 B5 R3 P4 D3

**Problem.** The uniformly spin-2 AKLT gap remains unproven on the diamond, kagome, and square lattices; the inscribed-square and triangle–octagon lattices are the only uniformly spin-2 cases with a certified nonzero gap.

**Theory of attack (salvaged — attack the memory wall, not the constant).** The binding constraint is not a constant-factor shortfall in the finite-size criterion; it is that spin-2 gives local dimension 5, so a subsystem large enough to satisfy the square-lattice threshold is 5^N with N in the twenties — an exponential wall. Do not enter the constant-improvement race. Instead: Pomata–Wei's boundary-transfer-operator formulation reduces the certification target to a **quasi-1D object**. A rigorous lower bound on the spectral gap of that transfer operator — via SDP relaxation with exact rational data, or Lanczos with interval arithmetic restricted to a symmetry sector, or a certified-truncation-error MPS/DMRG variational bound — is reachable at sizes direct 5^N diagonalization is not. That is a genuinely new certified computation and is the one input the crowded constant-improvement race lacks.

**First move.** Set up the Pomata–Wei boundary transfer operator for square-lattice geometry in exact rational arithmetic and establish a certified gap bound in the smallest symmetry sector, validating against a lattice where the gap is already proven. Separately, as a one-session pricing exercise: tabulate Knabe / Gosset–Mozgunov / Lemm–Mozgunov thresholds against best published certified subsystem gaps and compute the shortfall ratio — useful for pricing, not as a deliverable.

**Kill condition.** If certified interval-arithmetic bounds on the transfer operator degrade faster than the operator size grows — i.e. the certified bound is vacuous at every reachable sector size — the quasi-1D reduction does not buy anything and the problem is out of reach without new mathematics.

**Surviving objections.**
- The threshold-tabulation "crack" is not one: the square-lattice finite-size criterion has already been derived, and the published statement of the open problem is that the *memory* to certify the local gap at the required subsystem size exceeds current capacity. The first move as originally pitched returns a number already in the papers.
- The LTQO-import angle does not do what was claimed. Local-topological-quantum-order gap-stability theorems (Bravyi–Hastings–Michalakis lineage) prove an *existing* uniform gap survives perturbation — they take the gap as hypothesis. Importing them reproduces the hypothesis you are trying to establish.
- That angle is also occupied: arXiv:2605.12184 (2026) is exactly the LTQO graft, applied by the group that owns the tooling, to the hexagonal and Lieb lattices. You would be entering one lattice behind.
- The constant-improvement lineage (Knabe → Gosset–Mozgunov → Lemm–Mozgunov → Anshu) is multi-round and crowded, and a model brings no new certified computation to it.

**Yield: low, long shot.** Everything rests on whether certified numerics on the transfer operator stay non-vacuous. If they do, this is a genuine contribution; if not, nothing.

### 6. Beat — or bound — the Weaire–Phelan partition (Kelvin problem)
**Adjusted 16** (raw 24) · V4 C5 U2 B4 R2 P3 D4

**Problem.** No partition of space into equal-volume cells with surface area below Weaire–Phelan's 5.288 (per unit volume, normalized) has been found since 1993. Kusner–Sullivan proved WP beats anything with Kelvin topology; general optimality is wide open, and the best rigorous **lower** bound on minimal area per unit volume is very weak.

**Theory of attack (salvaged — take the partial credit as the deliverable).** Two defensible targets, neither of which is the record. (a) A delimited local-minimality/stability result: WP is a strict local minimum within the two-cell-type shape-parameter family, or within all partitions with cells of 12–16 faces at fixed topology. That is what the numerics can actually certify and it is publishable without any record falling. (b) Better: **improve the rigorous lower bound** on minimal area per unit volume. That is a real theorem with a page-scale certificate and a far better fit to the certificate economics than another sweep.

**First move.** Calibrate the checker before anything else: build the A15 Voronoi partition, equalize volumes, relax in Surface Evolver, and confirm 5.288; confirm Kelvin's truncated octahedron gives 5.306. Then set up the shape-parameter family around WP and establish the certified second-order/interval-arithmetic local-minimality statement.

**Kill condition.** If validation cannot reproduce 5.288 and 5.306 to three decimals, stop — no score is interpretable. If the local-minimality computation cannot be made rigorous (relaxation converges but interval bounds on the Hessian are vacuous), fall back entirely to the lower-bound direction or drop.

**Surviving objections.**
- Candidate supply is a fiction. Dodecagonal approximants (σ, Z, H) and most Frank–Kasper-adjacent block-copolymer/nanoparticle phases **are** tetrahedrally close-packed, and Kusner–Sullivan swept the TCP family. "Hundreds of candidates" is realistically five to ten distinct non-TCP structures — one batch, not a program.
- Non-TCP is disfavoured for a reason, not by oversight. The isoperimetric heuristic wants mean face count near 13.4, forcing 12/14/15/16-face cells — which is essentially the definition of TCP. Non-TCP candidates start with a structural area penalty.
- The input-conversion step, not the relaxation, is where these candidates die and it eats budget silently: crystallographic structures are sphere *centres* with unequal Wyckoff-site volumes, so equal-volume cells require Laguerre/weighted Voronoi with a volume-equalization solve that routinely fails to converge or converges to a different topology than intended.
- Kraynik, Weaire, Sullivan and collaborators have run exactly this pipeline over large catalogues of ordered and random monodisperse foams.

**Yield: medium, mostly the consolation prize.** Near-certain to produce a validated pipeline and a delimited stability statement. Near-certain *not* to beat 5.288. Tag every candidate TCP/non-TCP before relaxing anything and refuse to spend compute on the TCP ones.

## Tier 3 — Probes and bounded results, not projects

### 7. The last open ETP implication: E677 ⊧_fin E255
**Adjusted 13** (raw 19) · V5 C4 U1 B5 R2 P1 D1

**Problem.** The ETP final paper (arXiv:2512.07087): "we were unable to obtain either a human-readable or formalized proof or disproof of the implication E677 ⊧_fin E255." Tentatively conjectured false; resistant to every technique the project built. The unrestricted E677 ⊧ E255 was killed by a greedy construction.

**Theory of attack (salvaged — bet the other way).** The refutation direction is the one a large distributed project with a dedicated automated-reasoning stack already searched, at scale, past order 14 and across the structured families, without success. **Failed exhaustive search is Bayesian evidence for the positive direction**, and the original pitch had no plan for it. So: attempt E677 ⟹ E255 *for finite magmas* with the standard finite-magma toolkit — idempotent/pigeonhole arguments on iterated squaring, minimal-counterexample reduction, greedy-completion obstructions — targeting a Lean-formalizable proof against the existing statement. That is consistent with the search evidence and is where the ETP's own residual effort points.

**First move.** One hour on the positive direction: minimal-counterexample reduction plus pigeonhole on iterated squaring, checked against the Lean statement. Alongside, read the March 2026 "Mathematics Distillation Challenge – Equational Theories" submissions and the repo model-finding logs — any newly-swept structured family surfaces there first.

**Kill condition.** If the minimal-counterexample reduction produces no usable structure in the first session, leave. This is a probe with a pre-committed exit, not a project.

**Surviving objections.**
- Zero partial credit on either arm. Verified non-existence below order 20 is not a result; a failed proof attempt is not a result.
- The original first move ("read the appendix, find an unswept structured family") has an unfavourable structure: "was this family swept?" rarely has a crisp logged answer, and "demonstrably not covered" is a judgement the logs will not settle cleanly. The one-hour exit is optimistic.
- Tao's March 2026 distillation challenge points additional model-directed attention at precisely this instance. Marginal value of one more sweep is falling.

**Yield: near zero, by design.** Run only as a cheap, hard-exited probe.

### 8. Covering radius of RM(1,9): is max nonlinearity of a 9-variable Boolean function 242 or 244?
**Adjusted 11** (raw 19) · V5 C5 U1 B3 R2 P1 D2

**Problem.** Lower bound 242 (Kavut–Maitra, generalized rotation-symmetric and dihedral-symmetric classes); upper bound 244 (Hou). Nonlinearity 243 is impossible, so the answer is 242 or 244 and there is no middle. Unchanged since ~2006; no 2024–2026 paper narrows it.

**Theory of attack (salvaged — attack the upper bound).** The search lane is closed: 2^512 space, no partial credit, eighteen years of dedicated effort by the people who own the tooling. The one side where a certificate can exist and a single step closes the problem is the **upper bound**: improving Hou's bound from 244 to 243 resolves ρ(1,9) = 242 outright, since 243 does not occur. That is a finite arithmetic statement about integer vectors of length 512 and is plausibly Lean-formalizable. Second-best, with real partial credit: exhaustive non-existence of nonlinearity 244 within a **much larger structured class** than has been swept — e.g. all functions invariant under a maximal subgroup of GL(9,2), rather than just rotation and dihedral classes.

**First move.** Confirm 244 is still the best published upper bound and no sharper bound has narrowed the window. Then work the upper-bound side directly — Hou's norm/covering-radius argument and where its slack is — rather than the spectrum-counting side.

**Kill condition.** If Hou's bound has no identifiable slack at the 244→243 step, and the maximal-subgroup class enumeration is not computationally reachable, both lanes are closed — leave the same day.

**Surviving objections.**
- The moment-counting probe is dead on arrival, twice. Second moment: Parseval sum 262144 over 512 coefficients against a cap of 24 leaves 277+ admissible multisets using {24,20,16,0} alone — nowhere near infeasible. Fourth moment: `Σ W⁴` is the sum-of-squares indicator / differential-uniformity count, which is the **pruning heuristic of the existing rotation-symmetric searches** and is built into Hou's bounds already.
- The counting is aimed at the wrong object. Ruling out nonlinearity 244 requires excluding every Walsh *spectrum* (an assignment of integers to 512 points), not every admissible *multiset* of values. Moment identities constrain values, not placement, and there is no mechanism in them that reaches placement. Each surviving multiset would need its own combinatorial argument.
- The bent-concatenation bound for n = 9 is 240, so 242 is already an above-bound rarity; the search lane asks for a second such rarity in classes the same people already swept.

**Yield: near zero on the search, low but nonzero on the upper bound.** Only defensible as a targeted attempt on Hou's constant.

### 9. Andrews–Curtis: bounded-length non-trivializability for AK(3) and the residual Miller–Schupp presentations
**Adjusted 10** (raw 22) · V5 C3 U2 B4 R2 P3 D3

**Problem.** Whether AK(3) is Andrews–Curtis trivializable (unstably) is open; Shehper et al.'s sweep left a documented residue of Miller–Schupp presentations of length ≤ 7 that resisted trivialization. Note the literature hazard: Shehper et al.'s original 2024 claim that AK(3) is *stably* AC-trivial rested on a theorem later found to be incorrect; what certifies the result now is Lisitsa's explicit transformation sequences (arXiv:2501.18601, Jan 2025, Zenodo supplement).

**Theory of attack (salvaged — invert the deliverable).** The success-only asymmetry is fatal to a hunt: only success is certifiable, no invariant exists, and Havas–Ramsay plus the Shehper sweep already worked the bidirectional idea. So invert it. Run an **exhaustive, canonically-hashed BFS from AK(3)** (and from each residual Miller–Schupp presentation) under a hard total-length bound L, and publish the certified statement "not AC-trivializable within total length L" for the largest L reachable. That is bankable at every L, referee-checkable with a ~50-line independent checker, and precisely the form of result the area already publishes (Havas–Ramsay). Separately, mine the 8,634-move Miller–Schupp sequence for move-pattern heuristics to seed search on the residual length ≤ 7 cases, where the independent shots on goal actually are.

**First move.** Implement the AC-move checker and a canonical-form hash for balanced 2-generator presentations, validate by replaying a known trivialization, then run bounded BFS from AK(3) and record the largest certified L.

**Kill condition.** If canonical-form hashing at the frontier goes memory-bound before L exceeds the best published Havas–Ramsay bound, there is no new certified statement to bank — stop.

**Surviving objections.**
- The original first move rested on a misidentified object. The 8,634-move sequence is **not** a stable trivialization of AK(3); it is Lisitsa's ordinary (unstable) AC trivialization of a Miller–Schupp presentation MS₉(w*). It contains no stabilizing generator, so "measure the minimal word length achievable by local rewriting that avoids the stabilizing generator" is not a well-formed operation on it. The AK(3) stable sequences are a different object in a different paper.
- Even against the correct object, "rewrite the stable sequence to eliminate the stabilizing generator" is a restatement of the problem, not an angle on it: the extra generator functions as unbounded scratch space, which is exactly why the stable case is easy and the unstable case is not. And AC-move admissibility depends on the whole presentation, so step-local rewrites do not compose into a trajectory — the proposed "profile" produces a number with no theorem attached.
- Meet-in-the-middle is weaker than advertised: branching ≈ 12–24, so radius 8 from each side is ~10¹¹ nodes, and word lengths blow up along these trajectories.

**Yield: medium and near-certain, but small.** The bounded-length certified negative will land. It is a modest, real, publishable result whose value does not depend on any search succeeding. That is the whole case for picking it up.

### 10. Finite Rado numbers for nonlinear configurations (Hindman's {x, y, x+y, xy})
**Adjusted 5** (raw 17) · V5 C1 U2 B4 R2 P2 D1

**Problem.** Hindman's conjecture — every finite colouring of ℕ admits monochromatic {x, y, x+y, xy} — is settled for 2 colours (Bowen) and for all finite colourings of the nonzero rationals (Bowen–Sabok). **Three colours over ℕ is open in both directions.**

**Theory of attack (salvaged — calibrate on a configuration that terminates).** Do not attempt the 3-colour SAT campaign. Compute the first **finite Rado-type thresholds for the 3-element configuration {x, x+y, xy}** (Moreira's theorem; Alweiss gives effective bounds to sanity-check against) before touching the 4-element one. Publishing the first exact finite thresholds for nonlinear Rado-type configurations is a real, small, self-certifying result, and it yields an honest empirical scaling law from which to price the 4-element 2-colour and 3-colour cases rather than guessing.

**First move.** SAT-encode "no monochromatic {x, x+y, xy} in {2,…,N}" for 2 colours, binary-search the threshold against Alweiss's effective bound, then repeat for 3 colours if it terminates.

**Kill condition.** If even the 3-element 2-colour threshold runs past N ~ 10⁴ with solve times growing sharply, nonlinear Rado thresholds are not computable at any useful size and the whole line is priced out — same day.

**Surviving objections.**
- Certificate size is where this dies for the headline problem. Green–Sawhney (arXiv:2511.09365, Nov 2025) get only **tower-type** bounds for the strictly *easier* pattern {x+y, xy}. The 4-element system is harder and its extra constraints only bite for x, y ≤ √N, so its threshold cannot be better than tower-type. A DRAT/LRAT certificate at 3 colours is priced out by orders of magnitude; Boolean Pythagorean Triples at 200TB is a lower bound on hopelessness, not a reference point.
- Worse for the campaign framing: the 3-colour statement is **not known to be true**. A cube-and-conquer run may be hunting an UNSAT certificate for a satisfiable family, unable to distinguish "threshold astronomical" from "no threshold exists." The constraint hypergraph is sparse and locally tree-like except at divisor-rich integers — a positive-side signal for satisfiability.
- "Guaranteed finite by Bowen" gives finiteness with no bound: the ultrafilter/topological-dynamics arguments are non-effective, so there is no prior on where to binary-search.

**Yield: small but near-certain if you take the salvaged target.** Zero if you attempt the pitched one.

---

## Demoted — do not run as pitched

### 11. Persistence Conjecture for weakly reversible mass-action systems, dim(S) = 4
**Adjusted −80** (raw 25) · V4 C3 U3 B4 R3 P4 D4 · **carries a fatal objection; not formally killed only because a cheap salvage exists**

**Problem.** The Persistence Conjecture (weakly reversible mass-action systems do not have trajectories converging to the boundary) is open since 1974; dim(S) ≤ 3 is proved (Anderson, Pantea) by dynamical arguments.

**Why the pitched form is dead.** The bridge theorem was misused. Deshpande–Gopalkrishnan (arXiv:1309.3957) prove every minimal critical siphon is drainable *or* self-replicable, and that networks with no drainable siphon are persistent — and they state the difficulty is the **competition** between the two. The proposed target ("weak reversibility plus dim 4 forbids drainable critical siphons") is refuted by A ⇌ 2A: weakly reversible, {A} is a critical siphon, it is drainable (2A → A strictly decreases A), and the system is trivially persistent. Four disjoint copies give dim(S) = 4 with four drainable critical siphons. Worse, the proposed validation oracle — "dim ≤ 3 must return no drainable critical siphons" — is **false**, so a run would spend its time debugging correct code against a wrong oracle. There is also a one-line knockdown: weak reversibility is dimension-independent in statement, so the target lemma plus the bridge theorem would prove the full conjecture in every dimension, in one line.

**The only defensible remaining version.** Change the predicate, keep the pipeline. Enumerate weakly reversible dim(S) = 4 networks and search for critical siphons that are drainable **but not self-replicable** — the case Deshpande–Gopalkrishnan identify as the locus of difficulty. "Weak reversibility forbids drainable-but-not-self-replicable critical siphons" is a finite, LP-decidable statement that would actually imply persistence. Both predicates are LP feasibility tests on the same enumeration, so cost is unchanged, and the validation oracle becomes correct (dim ≤ 3 should return none). A dim-4 network with such a siphon is a genuine counterexample seed.

**Kill condition.** If drainable-but-not-self-replicable critical siphons are abundant in the first few hundred enumerated dim-4 networks, the combinatorial route is genuinely dead — and you learn it honestly inside the first hour.

**Yield: probably zero, but the first hour is cheap and self-diagnosing.** Take it only as an hour-long predicate check with a hard exit, never as a project.

---

## Killed during refutation — do not resurrect

**COSMIC mutational-signature non-identifiability certificate (SBS3/SBS5/SBS40)** — raw 30, killed for *demonstrated closure*. Two independent kills. (i) The claimed cross-domain move is published: MuSiCal (Nature Genetics 2024) is minimum-volume NMF — i.e. the Fu–Huang–Sidiropoulos sufficiently-scattered identifiability framework — applied to PCAWG expressly to resolve ambiguous flat signatures; the SBS3/SBS40 confounding is documented with cosine similarities and drove COSMIC's v3.4 split of SBS40 into 40a/b/c. (ii) The mathematics is internally inconsistent: with W pinned to COSMIC, small subsets of 96-vectors are linearly independent, so exposures are exactly unique and no non-monomial certificate exists; the proposed Q-transformation necessarily moves W off COSMIC, at which point the object is generic NMF non-uniqueness — constructible in closed form in minutes and dismissed by the field because WQ are not plausible biological signatures. The only live version is a *conditioning* statement (the identifiable exposure polytope at Poisson depth), which is a different, smaller problem.

**Ne vs. germline mutation rate — the three-way contradiction** — raw 27, killed for *demonstrated closure*. The circularity premise the entire attack rested on is contradicted by the source paper's own Methods: Bergeron et al. 2023 computed Ne uniformly by PSMC and state explicitly that "to avoid circularity, we estimated Ne based on the substitution rate calculated from the UCE alignment," noting a stronger signal *would* have appeared using the pedigree rate. The species-by-species provenance audit that was supposed to be the bottleneck resolves to one sentence already in print, and the pitch's own kill condition fires on reading the Methods. Separately the dispute has moved to generation-time mediation (PNAS 123(6), Feb 2026, 10.1073/pnas.2519649123, plus commentary 10.1073/pnas.2601432123) — a covariate-specification argument, i.e. exactly the war the errors-in-variables framing claimed to sidestep.

## What the top-ranked problems have in common

This is the reusable part. Every entry that survived with its value intact shares the same shape, and every entry that lost most of its value lost it to the same three mistakes. Both are stated below in a form that can be pasted directly into the next prospecting prompt.

**The shape that survives.**

> Look for open questions where (1) the field has an accumulating body of **sufficient** conditions and **no necessity/obstruction machinery at all** — this asymmetry is the single most reliable signal, because sufficiency is what constructive methods and automated search produce, so the necessity side is structurally under-attacked; (2) the deliverable is a **certificate a referee checks mechanically** — a Gröbner/ideal-membership witness, separating planes over a finite neighbour shell, a DRAT/LRAT proof, a Lean term, a multiplication table — so the run can know it succeeded without adjudication; (3) the object space is **finite and enumerable at a size you can state in advance** (graphs on ≤ 8 vertices, magmas of order ≤ 15, presentations of total length ≤ L, packings with ≤ k cells per period), so "we swept class C and found nothing" is itself the publishable result; and (4) there exists a **reformulation that turns an existential real-quantifier problem into ideal membership or LP feasibility at fixed low degree** — moments instead of eigenvalues, invariants instead of coordinates, transfer operators instead of full Hilbert space. Criterion (4) is what decides whether the computation terminates, and it is almost always the difference between a plan that runs and a plan that dies at "elimination did not finish."

**The three mistakes that cost the most points in this batch.**

> **(a) Assuming the space is unswept.** Four of eleven entries lost half or all of their value to a published algorithm that already outputs the objects the plan intended to find (twin-collapse graph search for FFD models; CEG's 16-tetrahedron periodic compressions; ETP's small-magma enumeration; MuSiCal's min-volume NMF). Before scoring "untried angle" above 2, search specifically for *an automated pipeline in the target literature*, not just for the result. The phrase "nobody has swept this programmatically" should be treated as a claim requiring a citation.
>
> **(b) Attacking a proxy for the real property.** Spectra instead of the operator algebra; convex hulls instead of the bodies; admissible multisets instead of full spectra with placement; drainable siphons instead of drainable-but-not-self-replicable ones. In each case the proxy is cheaper to compute and provably decides a different question. Check that the computed predicate is logically equivalent to the target property, on a worked example, before building anything.
>
> **(c) A kill condition that cannot fire.** Two entries specified early exits that arithmetic shows will pass — hull fill fraction ≥ 0.90 when the relevant motifs sit at 0.98; a second-moment count that leaves 277 admissible multisets. A kill condition should be *computed*, not asserted, at pitch time. A probe whose only possible outcome is "proceed" is not instrumented.

**Corollary for target selection.** Prefer problems where the negative direction is the deliverable. Record-beating framings ("find a denser packing," "find a better Boolean function," "find a new solvable model") have no partial credit and compete against decades of specialist tooling. The same infrastructure repointed at "certify that no object of this kind exists within this explicitly delimited class" is publishable at every class size, is self-certifying, and is the thing frontier models are actually differentially good at: exhaustive, error-prone, symbolic case analysis that humans avoid.
